bill.title: Falun Gong and Victims of Forced Organ Harvesting Protection Act
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 506.

industries.rationale: The bill would require financial institutions to block property and assets of sanctioned individuals and entities involved in forced organ harvesting.
The bill addresses organ transplantation practices and could affect medical institutions involved in international organ procurement or transplant tourism.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would impose visa restrictions and financial sanctions on foreign individuals involved in forced organ harvesting, particularly targeting persecution of Falun Gong practitioners. It would require the State Department to identify and report on individuals and entities participating in such practices, and would direct the President to block their property and deny them entry to the United States. The bill also calls for annual reports to Congress on implementation.

plain.whoItTouches: Mostly people outside the United States. It reaches most readers here only indirectly.

bill.title: HALT Fentanyl Act

industries.rationale: The bill changes registration and licensing requirements for pharmaceutical researchers conducting controlled substance research and affects the regulatory classification of chemical substances.
The bill establishes new criminal penalties and quantity thresholds that will affect prosecution and defense of drug trafficking cases.
Universities and research institutions conducting controlled substance research would be subject to the new registration processes and requirements established by the bill.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would permanently classify all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I controlled substances, meaning they would be treated as having high abuse potential and no accepted medical use. It sets the same criminal penalties and quantity thresholds for fentanyl-related substances as currently apply to fentanyl analogues. The bill also creates a streamlined registration process for researchers studying Schedule I substances and relaxes some requirements for research facilities working with controlled substances.

bill.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new content moderation obligations and 48-hour removal requirements on social media platforms and user-generated content websites.
New criminal prohibitions and mandatory restitution provisions would generate litigation and enforcement work related to intimate image publication.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would make it a federal crime to publish intimate images or videos of someone online without their consent, including computer-generated deepfakes, when the publication is intended to cause harm or involves a minor. Social media platforms and similar websites would be required to remove such content within 48 hours after receiving a complaint from the person depicted. Violators would face criminal penalties including prison time, fines, and mandatory restitution to victims.

bill.title: Combating Organized Retail Crime Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The bill directly addresses organized theft targeting retail operations and e-commerce platforms.
The bill explicitly covers theft from interstate and foreign shipments, affecting logistics and shipping companies.
The bill addresses online marketplaces and social media platforms where stolen goods are sold, potentially creating new compliance obligations.
The bill expands money laundering statutes to cover prepaid cards and gift cards, affecting payment processors and card issuers.

bill.plainSummary: This bill expands federal authority to prosecute organized retail theft and supply-chain crime. It allows prosecutors to aggregate the value of stolen goods over a 12-month period to meet felony thresholds, makes these offenses predicate crimes for money laundering charges, and authorizes asset forfeiture. The bill also creates a temporary coordination center within the Department of Homeland Security to help federal agencies work together on these cases.

bill.title: Laken Riley Act

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new detention mandates on DHS and creates liability exposure for federal agencies, while authorizing state governments to bring suit over immigration enforcement.

The bill creates new grounds for state litigation against the federal government and expands detention requirements, generating demand for legal services in immigration and intergovernmental litigation.

bill.plainSummary: This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security to detain certain non-citizens who are in the country unlawfully and have been arrested for or charged with crimes including burglary, theft, assault on law enforcement, or offenses causing death or serious injury. It also allows state governments to sue the federal government if immigration enforcement decisions or failures—such as releasing detainees, not conducting required asylum interviews, or violating parole limitations—cause harm to the state or its residents, including financial harm exceeding $100.

bill.title: A bill to amend the Higher Education Act of 1965 to require the standards for accreditation of an institution of higher education to assess the institution's adoption of admissions practices that refrain from preferential treatment in admissions based on an applicant's relationship to alumni of, or donors to, the institution, to authorize a feasibility study on data collection, and for other purposes.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

industries.rationale: The bill directly changes accreditation standards for colleges and universities, affecting their admissions policies and regulatory compliance obligations.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require accreditation standards for colleges and universities to evaluate whether institutions give preferential treatment in admissions to applicants who are children of alumni or donors (often called legacy admissions). It would also authorize a study on the feasibility of collecting data related to these admissions practices. The bill aims to change how accrediting bodies assess higher education institutions.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Federal Communications Commission relating to "Addressing the Homework Gap Through the E-Rate Program".

industries.rationale: The bill would eliminate a new revenue stream for wireless carriers and broadband providers who sell hotspots and mobile connectivity services to schools and libraries under the E-Rate program.
The bill would remove schools' and libraries' ability to purchase subsidized internet access equipment for students and patrons, affecting their budgets and service delivery.
The bill would affect manufacturers and vendors of Wi-Fi hotspot devices that would have been purchased through the expanded E-Rate program.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would overturn a Federal Communications Commission rule that allows schools and libraries to use E-Rate program funds to purchase Wi-Fi hotspots and mobile internet service for students and patrons to use at home. The FCC rule was designed to help students complete homework and access educational resources outside of school buildings. If this resolution passes, that rule would be nullified and schools and libraries would no longer be able to use E-Rate funds for off-campus internet access.

bill.title: A resolution supporting the goals and ideals of National Safe Digging Month.
bill.latestActionText: Submitted in the Senate, considered, and agreed to without amendment and with a preamble by Unanimous Consent. (consideration: CR S1789-1790; text: CR S1788)

industries.rationale: Electric and gas utilities own underground infrastructure that the resolution aims to protect through safe digging practices.
Telecom providers operate underground cable networks that could be damaged by excavation without proper location calls.
Construction firms and excavators are directly encouraged to use 811 services before digging projects.
Water and wastewater utilities maintain underground pipes that safe digging practices are designed to protect.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution expresses support for National Safe Digging Month and encourages homeowners and excavators to contact 811 before digging to locate underground utility lines. It is a non-binding resolution that does not change any laws or create new requirements. The measure promotes awareness of existing call-before-you-dig practices.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle and Engine Pollution Control Standards; Heavy-Duty Vehicle and Engine Emission Warranty and Maintenance Provisions; Advanced Clean Trucks; Zero Emission Airport Shuttle; Zero-Emission Power Train Certification; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision".
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

industries.rationale: The resolution directly affects heavy-duty vehicle manufacturers, trucking companies, and motor carriers by determining whether they must comply with California's stricter emission standards.
Automotive and engine manufacturers would face different regulatory requirements depending on whether California's waiver stands or is nullified.
Zero-emission vehicle mandates affect demand for electric vehicle charging infrastructure and clean energy services for commercial fleets.
Requirements for zero-emission trucks and airport shuttles would influence electricity demand and infrastructure investment for fleet charging.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would block an Environmental Protection Agency decision that allowed California to enforce its own stricter emission standards for heavy-duty trucks and engines. The EPA had granted California a waiver from federal preemption rules, permitting the state to require cleaner trucks, zero-emission airport shuttles, and advanced clean truck standards. If passed, the resolution would nullify that waiver and prevent California from implementing these regulations.

subjects: Hybrid, electric, and advanced technology vehicles

industries.rationale: Automotive manufacturers would face different regulatory obligations depending on whether California's distinct emission standards remain in effect.
The Advanced Clean Cars II regulations affect the market for electric vehicle charging infrastructure and clean-energy vehicle adoption.
Electric utilities face demand changes tied to electric vehicle adoption rates influenced by state emission standards.
Petroleum refiners and distributors face market impacts from regulations that affect the mix of gasoline versus electric vehicles sold.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn an Environmental Protection Agency decision that allowed California to enforce its Advanced Clean Cars II regulations. Those regulations set emission standards for vehicles sold in California that differ from federal standards. If passed, the resolution would nullify the waiver that permits California to apply its own rules.
